newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore Airlines issuing jet fuel tender mid-Nov.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Airlines issuing jet fuel tender mid-Nov.

text.p: Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA) is to issue its annual term purchase tender for aviation jet fuel in mid-November for its next financial year (April 1 1997-March 31 1998), industry sources said on Thursday. The tender is expected to close sometime between mid-and-end-December, 1996, they said.
The term contract would be for jet fuel liftings from 40 locations around the world and suppliers would be asked to quote prices for either one or two-year contracts, they said.
They said whether SIA would decide on one-or-two-year contracts would depend on how aggressively suppliers placed their offers.
Sources said the new tender would seek about 40 percent of SIA's estimated annual requirements of 950 million gallons (22.62 million barrels) of jet fuel.
They said SIA's annual jet fuel demand is increasing by about 8-10 percent, in line with its operational expansion.
But they noted the demand growth has been kept minimal because SIA's aircrafts are now more fuel-efficient while older aircraft have been replaced.

They also said SIA is still deliberating on whether to use the Far East Oil Pricing (FEOP) quotations in this tender along with the Platt's published price assessments. A decision would be made within two weeks, they said.
But they noted that there would not be any harm in allowing suppliers to use both quotations as this would give SIA the flexibility to decide on the most competitive prices.
Japan Airlines (JAL) is the only other airline using the FEOP quotes and the industry is closely watching whether SIA awards its tender using FEOP quotes.
SIA's new term tender comes at a time of escalating jet fuel prices and no respite is in sight as the market enters its peak demand season which runs into the first quarter of 1997.

SIA chairman and chief executive officer Cheong Choong Kong told Reuters on Wednesday that the airline, which traditionally hedges some of its jet fuel requirements, has not been able to hedge much for the second half of the year.
"All the experts were predicting fuel prices to come down in the second half," Cheong said in an interview with Reuters earlier this week.

"There was also expectations of Iraqi oil entering the market...but then things did not turn out. Then airlines started rushing in to try and lock in future prices which even exacerbated the situation. We have not been able to hedge -- it was too costly. Fuel prices were rising too fast," he said.
Cheong said that for the first half of SIA'a financial year ending September 30, 1996, it saved Singapore $20 million through its hedging activities.
Jet fuel cargos in Singapore are valued at $30.40 per barrel.
